title: Orthographic Skeletons: Can Children Start Learning How Words Are Spelled Before Theyve Seen it in Print
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick explores orthographic skeletons—invisible mental structures that form when children hear new words before encountering them in print. Drawing on research by Ataman, Beyersmann, Castles, and Wegener, the article demonstrates that oral vocabulary builds spelling expectations through phoneme-grapheme knowledge, creating a neural template that facilitates reading comprehension when words are later encountered in text. Multiple studies confirm this effect in both children and adults across inflected and derived word forms. The article argues this reframes the relationship between oral vocabulary and reading ability: knowledge isn't merely built through ambient exposure but through specific interactions between phonological and orthographic knowledge. Hendrick emphasizes that vocabulary-rich children arrive at school with hidden cognitive advantages—hundreds of pre-formed orthographic representations—while vocabulary-poor children lack these scaffolds, compounding the Matthew Effect in reading. He concludes that explicit, sequential vocabulary and phonics instruction must work in concert to build orthographic skeletons effectively.
points: Orthographic skeletons form when children's phoneme-grapheme knowledge generates spelling expectations for orally-learned words before encountering print.
The Matthew Effect in reading operates at the level of orthographic prediction: vocabulary-rich children form pre-learned word skeletons invisible to standard assessment.
Oral vocabulary and systematic phonics instruction are not competing priorities but two halves of the same cognitive mechanism.
Early, intensive vocabulary instruction has precision implications for reading equity unavailable through vague talk of word-rich environments.
Learning to read begins in the ear and mouth, not when the eye meets the page—prior knowledge reaches out to meet incoming text.

When both groups encounter the same text, one group is reading words their minds have been quietly preparing for. The other is meeting each word cold, with no prior expectation, no skeleton to ease the recognition process. This is the Matthew Effect in reading, but observed at a level of granularity that the usual discussions of “word gaps” and “literacy-rich environments” rarely achieve. The gap is not just one of exposure in the vague sense; it is a gap in the number of pre-formed orthographic representations stored in long-term memory.
